## What This Course Is

The AI Foundry is an AI-native product studio and consultancy. You are on a delivery team for a
paying client. The client is paying a fixed fee, retains the intellectual property, and expects
professional work. Your grade reflects both the quality of what you ship and the professionalism
with which you ship it.

We ship, not advise. Discovery work is real and comes first, but it exists to point at something
to build. Every engagement ends with software running in the client's hands, not with a deck.

This is a two-semester course. You enroll each semester. Engagements are accepted on a rolling
basis, so your team's phase boundaries come from your kick-off rather than from a course-wide
calendar.

## What You Give and What You Get

Joining the Foundry is a trade, and both sides of it are written down here so nobody has to
guess.

### What you give

| | |
|---|---|
| **Base commitment** | 10 hours per week, including the Friday studio block |
| **Surge commitment** | Typically an additional 10 hours per week when client demand calls for it |
| **Your tools** | You carry your own frontier AI subscriptions |
| **Your time horizon** | Two semesters, fall and winter |

The base 10 hours is the course. The surge hours are what real client delivery costs when a
deadline is real and the client is paying. Surge is not every week, and it is not open-ended,
but it is not optional either when your team is in it.

### What you get

**Three credits per semester, six across the year.** The credit is the compensation for the
base 10 hours. That is the academic side of the trade, and it is guaranteed whether or not your
engagement is a funded one.

**A stipend for the surge hours.** Credit pays for the base. Cash pays for the hours above it.
Foundry engagements are paid for by the client, and a defined share of that revenue comes back
to the students who did the work.

**Real work you can point at.** Production software running in a company's hands, shipped under
your name, with a client who will take your call.

### How stipends are calculated

Two inputs, and only two.

1. **The size of the stipend pool**, which is a published share of total Foundry revenue for the
   year. See the allocation table below.
2. **Your utilization**, which is your logged, verified hours on funded client work as a share of
   all such hours across the Foundry that term.

Your stipend is your utilization share of the pool. If you carried twice the load of a teammate,
you receive twice the stipend. Hours are logged weekly and confirmed by your team, and hours
that are not logged do not count.

A few things to be clear about:

- The stipend follows funded work. Students staffed only on pro bono or internal work in a given
  term do not draw from the pool for those hours.
- It is applied to your student account.
- This is a stipend, not employment. You are not an hourly employee of the university or of the
  client, and the stipend is not a wage or a guaranteed rate.
- Money applied to a student account can interact with a financial aid package. If you receive
  need-based aid, check with the financial aid office before assuming it is additive.

### Where the money goes

Not every dollar the Foundry earns goes back to Foundry members, and you should know what the
other dollars do. Revenue is allocated as a published waterfall:

| Claim | Share | Why it exists |
|-------|-------|---------------|
| Strategy program | 30%, capped at $100,000 per year | The Foundry sits inside the BYU strategy program, which provides the faculty, the classroom, the accreditation, and the students. The Foundry funds it back. |
| Reserve | 10% | Down years. A studio that cannot survive a slow semester cannot make commitments to clients or to you. |
| Program operations | 10% | Events, swag, travel to client sites and competitions |
| **Student stipend pool** | **The remainder, never less than 50%** | **You** |

Once the strategy program contribution reaches its $100,000 cap in a given year, every
additional dollar of that 30% flows into the student stipend pool instead. The cap is the point.
The Foundry funds the program that houses it, and then it stops taking.

These percentages are set for the year and published before engagements are staffed. They are
not adjusted after the fact.

## Studio Time

The Friday 8:00 to 11:50 AM block in 2140 TNRB is your team's standing work session:
co-working, cross-team critique, client calls, and office hours with Professor Murff.

**Required sessions:**

| Session | When |
|---------|------|
| Kick-off, team formation, client introductions | First studio of fall semester |
| Phase review: discovery | Set per engagement |
| Phase review: build | Set per engagement |
| Phase review: transfer and handoff | Set per engagement |
| End-of-year showcase | Final studio of winter semester |

Engagements start on a rolling basis, so phase reviews are scheduled per team rather than on a
single course calendar. Your team's review dates are set at kick-off and posted in Canvas.

All other Fridays are optional but strongly encouraged. Teams that skip studio time
consistently underperform.

## How You Are Assessed

Two instruments run alongside the point total, and they measure different things in different
ways.

**The Builder**, six axes: Discovery, Design, Application Architecture, AI Systems, Agentic
Workflow, and Launch and Learn. You self-report these at the start of fall semester and again in
December. They are **not graded**. They exist so you can see your own profile, so teams can be
staffed for coverage, and so the program can tell whether the year moved you.

**The Consultant**, four axes: Workstream Ownership, Client Presence, Communication, and
Collaboration.
These are what changes when the work belongs to someone else, and they are **not self-reported**.
The faculty advisor and your teammates rate them against observed behavior at midterm and at the
end of each semester, using the same 1 to 5 scale with written behavioral anchors.

The Consultant ratings inform the Client Evaluation and Peer / Team Evaluation components below.
They do not add points of their own.

| | Builder | Consultant |
|---|---|---|
| **What it measures** | What you can make | What changes when the work is for someone else |
| **Who rates it** | You | Faculty and teammates |
| **When** | September and December | Midterm and end of term |
| **Graded** | No | Feeds two existing components |

## Grading

Grades are based on weekly update emails, four milestone deliverables, client evaluation,
peer evaluation, and a video reflection.

### Grade Components (500 points possible)

| Component | Points | Weight |
|-----------|--------|--------|
| Weekly Update Emails | 140 pts | 28% |
| Milestone Deliverables | 160 pts | 32% |
| Client Evaluation | 100 pts | 20% |
| Peer / Team Evaluation | 60 pts | 12% |
| Video Reflection | 40 pts | 8% |
| **Base Total** | **500 pts** | 100% |
| Extra Credit (BYU Student Ratings) | 10 pts | +2% |

### Weekly Update Emails (140 points)

28 emails across two semesters, 5 points each.

| Status | Points |
|--------|--------|
| On time (Saturday by 11:59 PM) | 5 pts |
| Late (by Monday 12:00 PM noon) | 2 pts |
| After Monday noon | 0 pts |

See [Weekly Updates](03-weekly-updates.qmd) for format and expectations.

### Milestone Deliverables (160 points)

Four milestones, 40 points each. These are graded by the faculty advisor against the
[Build Standards](04-build-standards.qmd), not by the client.

| Milestone | What is due |
|-----------|-------------|
| **D: Discovery** | An AI-specific audit of the client's business. Where AI actually helps them, what is worth building, what is worth automating, with an estimate and a sequence. Client signs off. |
| **B1: Working build** | Software that runs, integrated with the client's systems or a realistic stand-in, with the architecture documented |
| **B2: Shipped** | Production code running in the client's environment. Tested, deployed, monitored |
| **T: Transfer** | Handoff documentation, a walkthrough with the client's own people, and a repository they can run without us |

Milestone due dates are set per engagement at kick-off and posted in Canvas. Teams on a
discovery-only engagement complete D and a scaled transfer; teams on a full engagement complete
all four.

Each milestone is scored on four dimensions, 10 points each:

| Dimension | What earns full marks |
|-----------|----------------------|
| **Correctness** | It works. Analysis reconciles, code does what it claims, assumptions are stated and defensible. |
| **Usefulness** | Someone at the client would actually use it. It solves the problem they have. |
| **Explainability** | Someone outside the team can follow how it works and why it does what it does. |
| **Craft** | Clean repository, readable code, tests where they matter, documents proofread, professional presentation. |

### Client Evaluation (100 points)

Your client point of contact evaluates the team twice: at mid-term for development only, and
at the end of the year as an input to your grade. Five dimensions on a 1 to 7 scale, listed
below. Faculty sends the client the same questionnaire both times, and you see the results.

| Category | Max Points |
|----------|------------|
| Timeliness | 20 |
| Communication | 20 |
| Agency | 20 |
| Technical Competency | 20 |
| Contribution | 20 |
| **Total** | **100** |

| Client Score (1-7) | Points |
|--------------------|--------|
| 7 | 20 |
| 6 | 17 |
| 5 | 14 |
| 4 | 11 |
| 3 | 9 |
| 2 | 6 |
| 1 | 3 |

The client scores the team. Individual adjustments come from peer evaluation.

### Peer / Team Evaluation (60 points)

Team delivery only works if the load is shared. Each teammate evaluates every other teammate
at mid-term and at the end of the year on four dimensions, 1 to 7 scale.

| Dimension | Question |
|-----------|----------|
| Reliability | They did what they said they would do, when they said they would |
| Quality | Their work did not need to be redone |
| Collaboration | They made the rest of the team more effective |
| Load | They carried a fair share of the hard work |

| Peer Score (1-7 average) | Points |
|--------------------------|--------|
| 7 | 15 |
| 6 | 13 |
| 5 | 11 |
| 4 | 9 |
| 3 | 7 |
| 2 | 4 |
| 1 | 2 |

::: {.callout-warning}
A student whose peer average falls below 3.0 at mid-term will meet with the faculty advisor.
Sustained free-riding is grounds for removal from the team and a failing grade, regardless of
what the client's team-level score says.
:::

### Video Reflection (40 points)

After receiving client and peer feedback, record a 2 to 5 minute video reflection.

**Due:** One week after end-of-year feedback is released

**Submission:** Upload to YouTube (unlisted) or Loom and submit the link via Canvas.

**Prompt:**

1. **Strongest area:** Which category best reflects your strengths this year? Give an example.
2. **Growth area:** Which category needs the most work? What got in the way?
3. **Client feedback:** React to one specific thing the client wrote. Do you agree? What will you do with it?
4. **Peer feedback:** What did your teammates tell you, and was it fair?
5. **Next time:** If you restarted this project knowing what you know now, what would you do differently?

Keep it conversational. I am looking for honest self-assessment, not polish.

**Rubric:**

| Criteria | Excellent (10) | Good (7) | Adequate (4) | Weak (0-2) |
|----------|----------------|----------|--------------|------------|
| **Self-awareness** | Accurately owns strengths and growth areas | Mostly accurate, somewhat surface | Vague or generic | Defensive or no insight |
| **Engages feedback** | References specific client and peer comments | Acknowledges feedback generally | Mentions feedback in passing | Ignores or dismisses |
| **Growth mindset** | Concrete plan for improvement | General intentions | Minimal forward-looking | No reflection on change |
| **Clarity** | Organized, right length, professional | Minor issues | Rambling or too brief | Unprepared or inappropriate |

### Extra Credit (10 points)

## Confidentiality and Client Data

Foundry clients share confidential business information: financials, pipelines, customer data,
and strategy. This is a condition of the work, and it carries obligations.

- You will sign the client's NDA, or the Foundry's standard mutual NDA, before receiving data.
- Client data stays in the approved project repository and approved tools. It does not go into
  personal accounts, personal cloud storage, or unapproved AI services.
- Nothing about the project goes on LinkedIn, in a portfolio, or in a job interview without
  written client permission. Ask the faculty advisor first, every time.
- Deliverables and intellectual property belong to the client, not to you and not to BYU.
- When the project ends, you delete local copies of client data.

A confidentiality breach is an Honor Code matter and will also end the engagement. Treat this
as the professional obligation it is.

## AI Use Policy

You are expected to use AI tools aggressively. That is the point of the Foundry. The
obligations that come with it:

- **You own the output.** "The model produced it" is not a defense for a wrong number, a
  fabricated citation, or an analysis you cannot explain.
- **Every deliverable must be explainable.** If you cannot walk the client through why the
  model recommends what it recommends, it is not done.
- **Client data goes only into approved tools.** See the confidentiality section above.
- **Disclose method, not apology.** Milestone documentation should say what tools and models
  you used and how you validated the output.

## Instructor Bio

Scott Murff is an Associate Teaching Professor of Strategy at the BYU Marriott School of
Business, where he also serves as faculty advisor and teaches courses on business strategy,
decision-making, and artificial intelligence. He brings over 15 years of experience at the
intersection of business and technology, having worked as a consultant, product manager, and
data scientist.

Prior to joining BYU, Scott spent nearly seven years at McKinsey & Company in roles ranging
from analytics specialist consultant to principal product manager, where he led product
development and performance management initiatives for Fortune 500 clients. His earlier career
includes building forecasting models as a VP at Zions Bancorporation and conducting regulatory
research at the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

Scott holds a Master's degree in Management Science & Engineering from Stanford University and
a B.A. in Economics with a minor in Math, from BYU. He is passionate about helping students
apply AI, analytics, and strategy to meaningful real-world problems with both rigor and purpose.

## Mission and Aims

The mission of Brigham Young University — founded, supported, and guided by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: is to assist individuals in their quest for perfection and eternal life. That assistance should provide a period of intensive learning in a stimulating setting where a commitment to excellence is expected and the full realization of human potential is pursued.

BYU seeks to develop students of faith, intellect, and character who have the skills and the desire to continue learning and to serve others throughout their lives.

A BYU education should be (1) spiritually strengthening, (2) intellectually enlarging, and (3) character building, leading to (4) lifelong learning and service.

Building on the foundational Mission and Aims, the Marriott School of Business aspires to transform the world through Christlike leadership by developing leaders of faith, intellect, and character guided by the following 4 values:

-   **Faith in Christ** - We value deep and abiding faith in Jesus Christ. Our faith gives us the capacity to envision a better future, the confidence to make that future happen, and the courage to act in the face of challenges.

-   **Integrity in Action** - We value integrity and hold ourselves to the highest moral and ethical standards. Acting with integrity builds trust, strengthens character, and focuses our ambitions on things of eternal consequence.

-   **Respect for All** - We value respect for all individuals as children of God and recognize the inherent worth, divine potential, and agency of each person. A climate of respect and belonging enhances our learning, facilitates collaboration, and encourages personal growth.

-   **Excellence** - We value excellence in learning, teaching, research, management, and leadership. An expectation of excellence magnifies our influence and motivates us to continually improve.

We evaluate our decisions and actions by the impact they will have on the academic experience, professional preparation, character development, emotional well-being, and spiritual growth of our students.

## Honor Code

In keeping with the principles of the BYU Honor Code, students are expected to be honest in all of their academic work. Academic honesty means, most fundamentally, that any work you present as your own must in fact be your own work and not that of another. Violations of this principle may result in a failing grade in the course and additional disciplinary action by the university. Students are also expected to adhere to the Dress and Grooming Standards. Adherence demonstrates respect for yourself and others and ensures an effective learning and working environment. It is the university's expectation, and every instructor's expectation in class, that each student will abide by all Honor Code standards. Please call the Honor Code Office at 422-2847 if you have questions about those standards.

## Preventing & Responding to Sexual Misconduct

The health and well-being of students is of paramount importance at Brigham Young University. If you or someone you know has experienced sexual harassment (including sexual violence), there are many resources available for assistance.

In accordance with Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, BYU prohibits unlawful sex discrimination, including sexual harassment, against any participant in its education programs or activities. The university also prohibits sexual harassment by its personnel and students. Sexual harassment occurs when

a person is subjected to unwelcome sexual speech or conduct so severe, pervasive, and offensive that it effectively denies their ability to access any BYU education program or activity; any aid, benefit, or service of BYU is conditioned on a person's participation in unwelcome sexual conduct; or a person suffers sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, or stalking on the basis of sex. University policy requires all faculty members to promptly report incidents of sexual harassment that come to their attention in any way, including through face-to-face conversations, a written class assignment or paper, class discussion, email, text, or social media post. Incidents of sexual harassment should be reported to the Title IX Coordinator at t9coordinator@byu.edu or (801) 422-8692 or 1085 WSC. Reports may also be submitted online at https://titleix.byu.edu/report or 1-888-238-1062 (24-hours a day).

BYU offers confidential resources for those affected by sexual harassment, including the university's Sexual Assault Survivor Advocate, as well as a number of non-confidential resources and services that may be helpful. Additional information about Title IX, the university's Sexual Harassment Policy, reporting requirements, and resources can be found at http://titleix.byu.edu or by contacting the university's Title IX Coordinator.

## Student Disability

Brigham Young University is committed to providing a working and learning atmosphere that reasonably accommodates qualified persons with disabilities. A disability is a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities. Whether an impairment is substantially limiting depends on its nature and severity, its duration or expected duration, and its permanent or expected permanent or long-term impact. Examples include vision or hearing impairments, physical disabilities, chronic illnesses, emotional disorders (e.g., depression, anxiety), learning disorders, and attention disorders (e.g., ADHD). If you have a disability which impairs your ability to complete this course successfully, please contact the University Accessibility Center (UAC), 2170 WSC or 801-422-2767 to request a reasonable accommodation. The UAC can also assess students for learning, attention, and emotional concerns. If you feel you have been unlawfully discriminated against on the basis of disability, please contact the Equal Opportunity Office at 801-422-5895, eo_manager@byu.edu, or visit https://hrs.byu.edu/equal-opportunity for help.
